title: Community and health
hookLine: attending services was linked to a lower risk of dying in a long study of nurses, and the cause is still debated (VanderWeele et al.)

lines: A FOLDING CHAIR, A PAPER CUP.
cards: A folding chair. A paper cup of coffee gone lukewarm. Someone you only see on weekends asks how your mother's knee is doing, because they remembered from last time.
Nothing about it is dramatic. It happens again next week, and the week after. Researchers wanted to know whether that kind of plain, repeated showing up does anything to a body over many years.
They found a link. Then came the harder question, still argued about: is it the showing up that does it, or something hiding behind it?

teach.b: First, the study. A team including Tyler VanderWeele looked at a long-running health study of nurses in the United States.
The nurses reported how often they went to religious services, and the researchers followed their health in the years after. Second, the finding.

teach.h: ATTENDING WAS LINKED TO LOWER RISK.
teach.b: Women who attended services more than once a week had a lower risk of dying during the study than women who never attended. Third, the honest part. Nobody assigned these nurses to go.
Maybe people who are already healthier go more often. Maybe going helps.

teach.h: A LINK, NOT PROOF OF CAUSE.
teach.b: The researchers adjusted for health, habits and other differences, and the link held.

But a study like this can't prove cause, and people still debate what might be doing the work: friends who notice when you're missing, a sense of meaning, fewer cigarettes, the steady rhythm of a week.
Fourth, two old lines about the same habit.
The Letter to the Hebrews, in the King James Bible, says: "Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is."
The reason it gives is encouragement, not a longer life: the next words are "but exhorting one another."
Jewish tradition keeps a neighboring teaching in the Sayings of the Fathers, where Hillel says not to separate yourself from the community. Neither text promises good health.
Both are about turning up for each other, week after week.

how: Religious communities gather weekly or more often for worship, and members often keep track of one another between services with visits, meals and calls.

o: a long study linking frequent service attendance to lower risk of dying
a rule that hospitals must offer religious services to nurses
proof that praying alone at home lengthens a person's life

games.q: you're a researcher. people who attend services often lived longer in your data. what do you say?
o: going to services causes longer life.
there's a link, and the cause is still open.
the link must be a fluke.
games.why: the team adjusted for many differences and the link held, but a study where nobody is assigned to attend can't settle cause.

practice: Bring to mind a group where your absence would be noticed, or could be: a congregation, a choir, a running club, a book group, the neighbors on one porch.
It doesn't need to be religious, and it doesn't need you to believe anything. See the door you'd walk through and one face on the other side, and let the breath carry that picture.

wordCard.voice: Community and health. In a long study of nurses, going to services often was linked to a lower risk of dying, and the reason is still debated. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, from Hebrews 10:25: the "assembling" together the letter urges people not to forsake.

carryVoice: Your line: show up. Somewhere, a folding chair has your name on it. Glad you came today.

sources.ref: Li, Stampfer, Williams and VanderWeele, "Association of religious service attendance with mortality among women" (JAMA Internal Medicine)
